\title{Reach-Based Sampling for Multi-Scale Localised Network Centrality}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
  Urban analysts measure street importance with localised network centrality (closeness and betweenness computed within a distance threshold) and compare results across places and cities. Computing centrality exactly traces shortest routes from every street and is costly at metropolitan scale, so analysts sample from a random fraction of streets. Sampling turns each street's score into a survey: its catchment is the population, and the sampled streets reaching it are the respondents. Because catchments vary by orders of magnitude, one uniform rate gives a sparse street too few respondents and oversamples a dense one, so uncertainty tracks density and undermines the cross-place comparison. Comparable uncertainty requires setting each street's precision from its own catchment size, its reach. Because reach is unknown, a cheap pilot poll measures every catchment by counting the routes that reach it. The poll is uncertain, so each street's rate is sized from a conservative lower bound on its reach, erring toward oversampling, and inverse-probability weighting keeps the estimate unbiased whatever the poll returns. Where sampling would not save time once the pilot is counted, the method computes exactly. Across four networks, with The Woodlands (TX) held out from calibration, both metrics preserve the ranking ($\rho \geq \adaptiveMinRhoFloor$) at 1--20\,km. On the held-out network the method computes closeness exactly, without sampling, whereas a fixed rate samples it and misses the target at 20\,km. Counting the pilot, sampled 20\,km runs are \adaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupMin--\adaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupMax$\times$ faster than exact computation. One tolerance parameter governs precision; the open-source \cityseer{} package implements it.
\end{abstract}

\textbf{Keywords:} network centrality, sampling, urban morphology, betweenness, harmonic closeness, computational efficiency

%==============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%==============================================================================

Urban morphological analysis relies on localised network centrality to reveal patterns of accessibility and flow in street networks \citep{Cooper2015}. Two measures are central to this work: \emph{closeness} (how easily a node can reach its neighbours) and \emph{betweenness} (how often a node lies on shortest paths between others). Both are computed within distance thresholds that range from pedestrian ($\approx$500\,m) to metropolitan ($\approx$20\,km) scales, as implemented in tools such as sDNA \citep{Cooper2018} and \cityseer{} \citep{Simons2022}.

Exact computation requires running a shortest-path traversal from every node; the cost scales with both the number of nodes and the size of each node's neighbourhood. A multi-scale analysis of the Greater London network (\glaNnodes{} nodes, plus a surrounding buffer; Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}) quickly becomes expensive: the exact 20\,km betweenness pass alone takes about seven minutes of multi-core compute (430\,s; Section~\ref{sec:setup}), and costs compound across thresholds and metrics.
% 430 s: GLA exact 20 km betweenness baseline; verified against output/gla_validation_adaptive.csv
% (sampled_time_b 27.69 s x speedup_betweenness 15.516 = 429.7 s), the same baseline tab7 divides.
% Re-verify if the macros are regenerated.
Sampling reduces this cost: traversals run from a randomly selected fraction of the nodes, and the results are scaled up. Each traversal visits every node within the threshold of its starting point, so a node's estimate is assembled from the traversals that reach it.

Sampling raises a difficulty of its own: comparability. Centrality patterns are routinely compared across areas and cities \citep{Strano2013}, and sampled estimates support that comparison only if they carry comparable uncertainty. Each node's score is a survey of its own \emph{catchment}, the set of nodes within the distance threshold. The precision of that survey depends on how many sampled sources reach the node, its \emph{reached sources}, which serve as the survey's respondents; the sampling rate matters only through that count. Catchment sizes vary by orders of magnitude between dense cores and sparse peripheries, so a fixed rate gives a dense district thousands of reached sources and a cul-de-sac a handful (Figure~\ref{fig:method_schematic}D illustrates the imbalance). Precision then tracks density within a city and between cities, so the estimates being compared carry unequal uncertainty. Existing adaptive methods do not close this gap. Methods such as KADABRA \citep{Borassi2019} tune their sample counts to a single network-wide accuracy target rather than to the precision of each catchment, and where distance-bounded variants exist they keep the same uniform target (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

When scores are computed within a distance threshold, the relevant population is the catchment, and catchments vary, so the sampling rate must be set per node from measured reach. We therefore measure every catchment with a cheap pilot poll: a small set of traversals is run from random starting points; a street with a large catchment is reached by many of them and a street with a small catchment by few, so each street's hit count measures the size of its catchment at every distance. Each node is then drawn as a traversal source with a probability sized to its own reach. A standard survey rule fixes how many respondents a population of a given size needs \citep{Eppstein2004}. Taking the node's catchment as that population, rather than the whole network, we divide the required number of respondents by the catchment's size (its reach) to get the chance that any one street is drawn as a sample source, its inclusion probability. Section~\ref{sec:method} states the full design: inverse-probability weighting for unbiasedness, a census for small catchments, a work test that selects exact computation where sampling cannot reduce cost, and a shared traversal that serves both metrics from one sample.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A localised sample-size bound: under a distance threshold the relevant population is the catchment, whose size is the reach $r$ rather than the network size $n$, so the required samples scale with $\log r$ rather than $\log n$.
  \item A per-node sampling design with a single tolerance parameter $\varepsilon$: a pilot poll measures every catchment, each node receives an inclusion probability sized to a confidence bound on its reach, inverse-probability weighting keeps estimates unbiased, and a per-distance work test selects exact computation where sampling cannot reduce cost.
  \item Empirical validation at 1--20\,km on four street networks spanning the urban density range, one held out from all accuracy calibration, together with an ablation that replaces the measured reach with cheaper stand-ins and shows assumed reach failing exactly where the reach measurements predict.
  \item An open-source implementation in the \cityseer{} Python package.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} defines the centrality measures and the evaluation target. Section~\ref{sec:method} states the method. Section~\ref{sec:ablation} presents the ablation: three ways to know a catchment's size, and why measurement is necessary. Section~\ref{sec:validation} reports the validation. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} covers practical guidance, the scope of the guarantee, limitations, and related work; Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

%==============================================================================
\section{Preliminaries}
\label{sec:preliminaries}
%==============================================================================

Both centrality measures are computed with a distance cutoff $d_{\max}$. We write $d$ for $d_{\max}$ when the context is clear.

\paragraph{Harmonic closeness.}
Closeness measures how easily a node can reach its surroundings \citep{Freeman1979}. We adopt the \emph{harmonic} form, a sum of inverse distances over reachable nodes, rather than classic closeness, the reciprocal of summed distances. A distance threshold leaves most of the network unreachable, and classic closeness is ill-defined or unstable on the resulting disconnected, variably sized catchments. Harmonic closeness sums bounded per-node contributions, with unreachable nodes contributing zero, so it stays well-defined and comparable across catchments of different size while capturing the same notion of accessibility as classic closeness \citep{Rochat2009, Boldi2014}. The additive form is also what lets a single source's contribution be estimated independently under sampling (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}). For each node $v$ it sums the inverse distances to all nodes within the threshold, so nearby nodes contribute more than distant ones:
\begin{equation}
  C_H(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{u \neq v \\ d(v,u) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{1}{d(v, u)}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Betweenness.}
Betweenness measures how often a node acts as an intermediary \citep{Freeman1977}. For each node $v$, it sums, over all pairs of other nodes within the threshold, the fraction of that pair's shortest paths that pass through $v$:
\begin{equation}
  C_B(v;\, d_{\max}) = \sum_{\substack{s \neq t,\; s \neq v,\; t \neq v \\ d(s,t) \leq d_{\max}}} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}}
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_{st}$ is the total number of shortest paths from $s$ to $t$, and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ is the number that pass through $v$. On undirected graphs each pair of endpoints is counted once (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_betw} gives the ordered-pair weighting). Any piece of a shortest path is itself a shortest path, so a distance-bounded traversal from each source discovers every node that could contribute to betweenness at that threshold; this property is what lets the sampling design of Section~\ref{sec:method} serve betweenness from the same traversals as closeness. The subpath property holds for shortest-path (metric) distance. It need not hold for angular (simplest-path) distance \citep{Turner2007}, which scores routes by how much they turn rather than how far they run; Section~\ref{sec:limitations} returns to that case.

\paragraph{Reach.}
The set of nodes within distance $d$ of a node $v$ is $v$'s \emph{catchment}; the \emph{reach} of $v$ is its size, $r_v = |\{u : d(v,u) \leq d\}|$. Reach grows roughly with the square of the analysis distance, and at any fixed distance it scales with local node density, so it varies by orders of magnitude between dense cores and sparse peripheries. A per-node sampling rate must track that variation. In the survey analogy reach is the population size. The three components of the method introduced in Section~\ref{sec:method} each take reach as their input: the pilot poll measures it, each node's sampling probability is set from it, and the work test prices the cost of computation against it.

\paragraph{Buffers and live nodes.}
Nodes near the edge of a network have artificially low centrality because their neighbourhoods are truncated. The standard remedy \citep{Gil2017} is to surround the study area with a ring of \emph{buffer nodes}: paths can pass through them, but their own centrality values are not reported. Only the interior (\emph{live}) nodes receive results. In survey terms, people living just outside a district still answer questions about streets inside it, but their own streets are not scored. We write $n_L$ for the live count, $n$ for the total, and $\varphi = n_L / n$ for the live fraction.

\paragraph{Accuracy metric.}
We evaluate sampling quality using Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$) between sampled and exact centrality values. Urban applications rely on relative rankings (e.g., identifying the most central streets) rather than absolute values, so $\rho$ captures the quantity of practical interest. We set the target at $\rho \geq \targetRho$, a conventional threshold for ranking applications; a looser $\rho = 0.9$ would allow visible reordering among the lower-ranked streets. A validation \emph{cell} is one combination of network, metric, and distance. Two numbers from the sampled 20\,km cells make that target concrete: the median street moves by at most \sampledMedianShiftMax{} percentile points in the ranking, and at least \sampledTopDecileRetentionMin\% of the streets that truly fall in the most-central tenth stay there.

%==============================================================================
\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
%==============================================================================

The method is a survey. Each street's score is estimated over its own catchment, so each catchment is a population, and each population needs its own sample size. The population sizes are unknown, so a cheap poll measures them first; the survey proper is then sized street by street. Three questions organise the section: how many samples a population of a given size needs (Section~\ref{sec:bound}), how big each population is (Section~\ref{sec:pilot}), and when a census is cheaper than a survey (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}).

\subsection{How many samples does a catchment need?}
\label{sec:bound}

Following \citet{Eppstein2004}, sources are drawn at random, a distance-bounded shortest-path traversal runs from each, and each sampled contribution is scaled up by the reciprocal of its inclusion probability (inverse-probability weighting; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}). In survey terms, a respondent who had a 1-in-10 chance of being asked speaks for ten people.

Hoeffding's inequality \citep{Hoeffding1963} is the survey's margin-of-error rule: it states how many respondents keep an estimate within a stated tolerance. The respondents for a target $v$ are its \emph{reached sources}, the sampled sources whose traversals reach $v$; all of them lie in $v$'s catchment. Consider first an idealised survey of that catchment: $k$ sources drawn uniformly at random from the $r_v$ catchment members, each contribution weighted by $r_v / k$. The estimate $\hat{C}_H(v)$ is then a sum of $k$ bounded terms, and Hoeffding's inequality, which covers draws without replacement, gives
\[
  \Pr\!\left[\left|\hat{C}_H(v) - C_H(v)\right| > \varepsilon \cdot C_{\max}\right] \leq 2 \exp(-2k\varepsilon^2),
\]
where $C_{\max}$ bounds the total centrality attainable over the catchment. For harmonic closeness $C_{\max} = r_v / d_{\text{near}}$ suffices, where $d_{\text{near}}$ is the smallest distance from $v$ to a catchment member; each weighted term then lies in $[0, C_{\max}/k]$. $C_{\max}$ can be large where a neighbour sits close to $v$, so a tolerance stated relative to $C_{\max}$ can be loose in absolute terms; Section~\ref{sec:guarantee_scope} discusses this looseness. Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht} restates the per-term bound for the deployed design of Section~\ref{sec:pilot}, where a floor on the sampling probabilities bounds the weights.

The required $k$ follows from the failure budget $\delta$, the survey's total allowance for streets whose estimates miss the tolerance; covering every street means splitting that allowance among them. In the global setting of \citet{Eppstein2004} the guarantee is extended to all $n$ nodes of the network by dividing the failure budget $\delta$ across them (a union bound), which puts a $\log n$ factor into $k$. Under localisation only the catchment matters, so the failure budget is divided across the $r_v$ members of $v$'s own catchment instead: a target surveyed at the resulting rate fails with probability at most $\delta / r_v$. Solving $2r\exp(-2k\varepsilon^2) \leq \delta$ for $k$ gives the required reached-source count for a catchment of size $r$:
\begin{equation}
  k(r) = \frac{\ln(2r/\delta)}{2\varepsilon^2}.
  \label{eq:hoeffding_k}
\end{equation}
Where reach is locally homogeneous (nearby nodes have catchments of similar size), this allocation carries a catchment-scale analogue of the global guarantee: a catchment holds roughly $r_v$ nodes, each failing with probability at most $\delta / r_v$, so the expected number of nodes in any one catchment that exceed the tolerance is at most $\delta$. At the default $\delta = \hoeffdingDelta$, that expected count is at most \hoeffdingDelta{} tolerance-exceeding nodes per catchment. The count scales with $\log r$ rather than $\log n$.

Two parameters enter the bound: the tolerance $\varepsilon$ and the failure probability $\delta$. The failure probability is held at its default throughout, so $\varepsilon$ is the single calibrated parameter governing precision (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}); the work test of Section~\ref{sec:worktest} adds one empirically chosen cost constant. At the default $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$, a catchment of 40{,}000 nodes requires roughly 2{,}700 reached sources.

One sample can serve betweenness as well as closeness at almost no extra cost. Each source already runs a distance-bounded Dijkstra traversal (the standard shortest-path algorithm), and Brandes' backpropagation \citep{Brandes2001} recovers the source's betweenness contributions from that same search tree. Reusing the closeness sample for betweenness is a computational choice; the closeness bound does not entail it, so the adequacy of one sample for both metrics is established empirically (Sections~\ref{sec:validation} and~\ref{sec:guarantee_scope}).

\subsection{How big is each population? The pilot poll}
\label{sec:pilot}

The bound of Section~\ref{sec:bound} describes an idealised fixed-size survey of each catchment. The deployed design approximates that survey; this section states the design and returns to the gap between the two. The catchment sizes are unknown, so a pilot polls them. The pilot draws $m = \min(n,\, \max(400,\, 0.025\,n))$ sources uniformly and runs one distance-bounded Dijkstra from each, out to the largest requested threshold. On an undirected network the probability that a uniformly drawn source lies within distance $d$ of node $u$ equals $r_u(d)/n$, so $u$'s hit count over the $m$ pilot traversals estimates its reach. (The pilot draws without replacement, so its hit counts sit slightly more tightly around the truth than independent draws would; the confidence bounds introduced below therefore stay on the conservative side \citep[Theorem~4]{Hoeffding1963}.) One traversal set therefore measures every catchment at every distance, and because the poll travels on the network itself, it respects rivers, railways, dead ends, and disconnected fringes.

The two directions of estimation error carry different costs. An overestimated reach undersamples the catchment, which risks accuracy; an underestimated reach only oversamples it, which costs time. Inclusion probabilities therefore derive from a one-sided lower confidence bound on reach (an exact binomial confidence bound: Clopper--Pearson at $\alpha = 0.1$; \citealp{Clopper1934}), written $\hat{r}^{-}_u$:
\begin{equation}
  q_u = \min\!\left(1,\; \frac{k(\hat{r}^{-}_u)}{\hat{r}^{-}_u}\right),
  \label{eq:node_q}
\end{equation}
floored at $q_u \geq 0.01$ to bound the inverse-probability weights at 100. A node the poll rarely hits falls toward $q = 1$: when the poll cannot establish that a population is large, that population is surveyed in full. Saturation at $q = 1$ is a census of sparse catchments and is exact for them. Contributions are weighted $1/q_u$ per source (Horvitz--Thompson weighting, the standard name for this inverse-probability weighting; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}), so estimates are unbiased whatever the pilot's quality; pilot error affects precision and running time, not bias.

The deployed probabilities give each target the respondents its reach calls for wherever reach is locally uniform, and fall short only at the edge of a dense district. A target $v$ is answered by the members of its catchment, each drawn as a source with its own probability, so $v$'s expected count of reached sources is the sum of those probabilities. Each $q_u$ is sized to the source's own reach rather than to $v$'s, so the count matches $k(r_v)$ only when the two agree. Where reach is locally homogeneous they do: the catchment members share $v$'s reach, and probabilities set at the true reach would deliver exactly $k(r_v)$ expected respondents, $r_v$ members each with probability $k(r_v)/r_v$. Because the pilot's lower confidence bound normally sits below the true reach, it raises each $q_u$, and the expected count $\sum_{u:\, d(v,u) \leq d} q_u$ meets or exceeds $k(r_v)$ (Figure~\ref{fig:method_schematic}C: 22 reached sources against the required 18); the exception is the small tail where the pilot overestimates reach, with probability at most $\alpha$ per node. The shortfall shows at the boundary of a dense district: such a street is answered mostly by streets inside the district, whose large catchments earned them low sampling probabilities, so it can collect fewer than the $k(r_v)$ respondents its own reach calls for. Saturation at $q = 1$ around sparse nodes limits the shortfall, and the residual effect is assessed empirically (Section~\ref{sec:error_structure}).

The poll size $m$ affects cost, not correctness. A smaller $m$ widens the confidence bounds, which pushes $q$ toward 1 and the work test (below) toward exact computation; both directions are conservative. The pilot parameters (the $m$ rule, $\alpha = 0.1$, the probability floor) are fixed conventions of the implementation; none is fitted to a validation network. The work test below adds one further constant, the work-test margin (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}).

This deployed design differs from the idealised survey of Section~\ref{sec:bound}. It does not pick exactly $k(r_v)$ respondents per street: every catchment member is included or not by its own independent draw, so the realised reached-source count varies around the expected count (Figure~\ref{fig:method_schematic}C), and the inverse-probability weights vary across sources. The idealised bound is therefore an approximation for the deployed estimator. The probability floor bounds the weights, and the approximation is assessed empirically (Sections~\ref{sec:guaranteed_vs_validated} and~\ref{sec:validation}).

\subsection{When is a census cheaper? The work test}
\label{sec:worktest}

When a population is small, a census is cheaper than a survey. The same holds for a whole distance threshold: at short distances traversals are cheap and sampling saves nothing, so the implementation must decide, per distance, whether to sample at all.

A \emph{call} is one request for a set of metrics and distances. Which streets must run a traversal depends on the metric and on whether it is computed exactly or by sampling, so the work test prices the cost of exact work separately for each metric. Exact \emph{closeness} is a census: each live street tallies its own neighbours from its own traversal, so only the $n_L$ live streets run. Sampled closeness is a survey: a street's score is assembled from other streets' traversals under inverse-probability weighting, so streets just outside the boundary must be eligible sources, or boundary streets lose their contributions. \emph{Betweenness} runs from every node in either mode. A shortest path between two buffer nodes can pass through a live interior node, and that interior node must receive credit for lying on the path, so buffer nodes must serve as sources too. The work test compares predicted traversal work, where each source's work is proportional to the size of the neighbourhood it explores, and selects sampling only when the predicted sampled work falls below a margin $\gamma = 0.75$ of the predicted exact work:
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{u \in V} q_u\, \hat{r}^{+}_u \;<\; \gamma \cdot
  \begin{cases}
    \sum_{u \in V_L} \hat{r}^{+}_u & \text{(closeness only)}\\[2pt]
    \sum_{u \in V} \hat{r}^{+}_u  & \text{(betweenness requested).}
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:work_test}
\end{equation}

Work is priced from the \emph{upper} confidence bound $\hat{r}^{+}_u$: a node the poll never hit is censused at $q = 1$, so pricing its traversal at a point estimate of zero would select sampling in cases where exact computation is cheaper. The work model counts traversal nodes and omits the fixed overheads: the pilot itself, the per-node random draws, and the weighting arithmetic. The pilot is the largest of these, and in a multi-distance call it is shared across all distances and both metrics, so the model does not charge it to any single distance; the measured wall-clock speedups, by contrast, include it.

The margin $\gamma$ exists to cover this omitted overhead. It was set from realised timings in preliminary runs on the four validation networks made without a margin, where cells with predicted work ratios between 0.8 and 1.0 ran slower than exact computation; $\gamma = 0.75$ holds sampling back until the predicted saving is large enough to survive the overhead. It is the one empirically chosen constant besides the tolerance $\varepsilon$ (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}), and it affects only whether sampling engages, not the per-node probabilities or the resulting estimates. Because the overhead it absorbs is only approximate, a cell the test approves for sampling can realise a smaller speedup than its predicted work ratio implies; in the validation every sampled cell nevertheless runs faster than exact computation (Section~\ref{sec:validation}).

Sampled closeness carries a built-in handicap: it must be able to draw sources from every node, live or buffer, whereas exact closeness runs a traversal only from each live node and is therefore already cheap. On networks with a low live fraction $\varphi$ this handicap outweighs any sampling saving, so the work test routes closeness-only calls to exact computation. On Cary at 20\,km, for example, exact closeness prices only the live fraction of nodes as sources ($\varphi = \caryLiveFraction$), the predicted sampled work exceeds $\gamma = 0.75$ of that exact cost, and closeness runs exact. The per-node probabilities fall low enough to overcome the handicap only on dense networks at long distances, so closeness sampling engages there. Betweenness, by contrast, runs from all nodes in both modes, so its decision turns on the probabilities alone: London's 20\,km betweenness prices every node as an exact source, sampling is predicted cheaper, and it runs at a measured \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ (Section~\ref{sec:validation}).

The test runs once per call and per distance: a call that requests betweenness prices exact work over all nodes, and a closeness-only call prices it over the live nodes, a stricter test. We call the resulting per-distance decision the \emph{mode} of that computation: exact or sampled. A single-metric call therefore carries its own mode; a call that computes both metrics together applies the with-betweenness pricing to both.

\subsection{Algorithm and worked example}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:adaptive} states the procedure; Figure~\ref{fig:method_schematic} illustrates it on a worked example. In the implementation, distances routed to exact computation are batched, so a single Dijkstra per source serves all of them; each sampled distance runs its own pass under its own per-node probabilities.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
  \caption{Per-node reach-based sampling for localised network centrality}
  \label{alg:adaptive}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Require Network $G = (V, E)$ with live nodes $V_L \subseteq V$ and buffer nodes $V_B = V \setminus V_L$
    \Require Distance thresholds $D = \{d_1, \ldots, d_j\}$
    \Require Tolerance $\varepsilon$ (default $\hoeffdingEpsilon$), failure probability $\delta$ (default $\hoeffdingDelta$), poll level $\alpha$ (default 0.1), work-test margin $\gamma$ (default 0.75)
    \Ensure Closeness estimates $\hat{C}_H[d]$ and betweenness estimates $\hat{C}_B[d]$ for each $d \in D$

    \State Pilot: draw $m = \min(|V|,\, \max(400,\, 0.025\,|V|))$ sources uniformly; run one Dijkstra per source, bounded at $\max(D)$; record per-node hit counts $h_u[d]$ for each $d \in D$
    \For{each distance $d \in D$}
    \State Reach bounds: $\hat{r}^{-}_u,\, \hat{r}^{+}_u \gets$ one-sided Clopper--Pearson bounds from $h_u[d]$ at level $\alpha$
    \State Per-node probability: $q_u \gets 1$ if $\hat{r}^{-}_u = 0$ (census); otherwise $q_u \gets \min\!\left(1,\; \ln(2\hat{r}^{-}_u/\delta) \,/\, (2\varepsilon^2\, \hat{r}^{-}_u)\right)$, floored at 0.01
    \State Work test: exact cost $\gets \sum_{u \in V_L} \hat{r}^{+}_u$ (closeness only) or $\sum_{u \in V} \hat{r}^{+}_u$ (with betweenness)
    \If{$\sum_{u \in V} q_u \hat{r}^{+}_u \geq \gamma \cdot$ exact cost} \Comment{a census is cheaper; Section~\ref{sec:worktest}}
    \State Run exact computation (closeness sources $V_L$; betweenness sources $V$)
    \Else
    \State Sample sources $S \subseteq V$ by including each node $u$ independently with prob.\ $q_u$
    \For{each source $u \in S$} \Comment{$S$ includes both live and buffer nodes}
    \State Run distance-bounded Dijkstra from $u$
    \State Accumulate closeness to each live target $v$ via $1/(q_u \cdot d(u,v))$ \Comment{IPW}
    \State Run Brandes backpropagation; accumulate betweenness for live targets, weighted $1/q_u$
    \EndFor
    \EndIf
    \EndFor

    \State \Return $\{\hat{C}_H[d],\, \hat{C}_B[d] : d \in D\}$
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

  \centering

C) One random draw under these probabilities. The dense catchment receives 22 reached sources (sampled sources falling inside the catchment, labelled $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$) against the required 18. The 14-node catchment saturates: $k$ exceeds its population, so its requirement is a census of all 14 nodes, and the draw includes 13 of them (a few members near the core carry $q$ below 1). The fixed rate is set to $k/\bar{r} = 0.20$, the rate sized for a catchment of average reach, so the two designs spend a comparable overall budget.}
\label{fig:method_schematic}
\end{figure}

\subsection{What is guaranteed and what is validated}
\label{sec:guaranteed_vs_validated}

The design separates three levels of assurance. Unbiasedness is guaranteed for both metrics by the Horvitz--Thompson weighting, independently of pilot quality (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix_ht}). The additive error guarantee of Section~\ref{sec:bound} applies to closeness and is stated for the idealised fixed-size survey of each catchment; the deployed probabilities are sized so that each target's expected reached-source count meets $k(r_v)$ under locally homogeneous reach (Section~\ref{sec:pilot}), and the gap between the idealised and the deployed design is assessed empirically. Rank fidelity, the quantity applications rely on, has no formal bridge from the additive bound and is validated empirically (Section~\ref{sec:validation}). Betweenness has no comparable per-source bound. A single source can account for a large share of a target's betweenness, and these per-source contributions vary far more from source to source than closeness contributions do, so betweenness is judged entirely by the validation.

%==============================================================================
\section{Ablation: why measurement is necessary}
\label{sec:ablation}
%==============================================================================

The load-bearing component of the method is the measurement of reach. This section tests it by ablation: the measured reach is replaced with cheaper stand-ins. There are three ways to know a population's size: assume it from a formula, count it on a map, or measure it on the network. The first two rungs each fail in a way the next catches.

\subsection{Rung 1: assume reach from distance}
\label{sec:canonical}

A network-agnostic schedule can be built by assuming a single reach value per distance. On a regular grid with inter-node spacing $s$, the number of nodes within distance $d$ is the area of a circle divided by the area per node:
\begin{equation}
r_c = \frac{\pi d^2}{s^2}.
\label{eq:canonical_reach}
\end{equation}
We call this the \emph{canonical reach}. With $s = \gridSpacing$\,m, Eq.~\ref{eq:hoeffding_k} yields one fixed sampling rate per distance, $p(d) = \min(1, k(r_c)/r_c)$, shared by every node at that distance. The spacing is deliberately conservative: it sits above typical mean street-segment lengths in European cities (city means $\approx$95--122\,m; \citealp{Strano2013}), and a larger $s$ lowers the assumed reach and so raises the sampling rate, erring toward oversampling. The single free parameter, the tolerance $\varepsilon$, was calibrated once on the sparsest calibration network (Cary, NC), where the grid model is least conservative; $\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$ is the loosest value at which Cary meets the $\rho \geq \targetRho$ target at every distance. The per-node method of Section~\ref{sec:method} inherits this $\varepsilon$ unchanged. The only other empirically chosen constant is the work-test margin (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}), which affects when sampling engages, not how much is sampled.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/fig6_reach_comparison.pdf}
\caption{Ablation rung 1: mean measured reach vs.\ analysis distance (logarithmic axes) for the four validation networks, against the canonical grid model ($s = \gridSpacing\,$m, grey line). Background tints mark the regions above and below the canonical curve. The dense metros lie at or above the canonical curve, so the canonical schedule oversamples them. The suburbs lie below it: the grid model overestimates their reach, and the schedule under-samples them. The held-out Woodlands network lies lowest, which predicts its failure (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}). The annotated arrow marks the held-out network's 20\,km gap, where the assumed reach is 2.6 times the measured value.}
\label{fig:val_reach}
\end{figure}

The assumption fails where real reach falls below the curve (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}). Table~\ref{tab:ablation} condenses the canonical schedule's record on the four networks; the per-distance detail is in Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:validation}--\ref{tab:woodlands_validation}. The three networks available during calibration (London, Madrid, Cary) meet the target at every distance. The held-out network fails at the one distance where sampling engaged for its closeness: 20\,km, with $\rho = \woodlandsMinRho$ against the $\targetRho$ target. (At shorter distances the suburbs' low live fractions keep closeness in exact mode, so those rows are exact by construction and say nothing about estimation quality.) The failure has a mechanistic explanation: at 20\,km The Woodlands reaches \woodlandsReachRatioTwentyKm{} of the canonical reach, against \caryReachRatioTwentyKm{} for Cary, so the canonical schedule under-samples it more severely than any network used in calibration. A post-hoc sweep confirms the diagnosis: re-running the held-out network at a tighter tolerance ($\varepsilon = 0.04$) restores the target, so the failure is under-sampling from overestimated reach rather than a defect of the bound. The canonical schedule carries no information about an individual network's reach; the measured reach identifies the deficit before any centrality run.

\input{tables/tab8_ablation}

\subsection{Rung 2: count reach on a map}
\label{sec:euclidean}

A cheaper measurement counts, for each node, the neighbours within the Euclidean radius (a KD-tree query, no network traversal), then divides by a fixed deflation factor of 2.5, because Euclidean discs hold more nodes than network catchments of the same radius. The deflation is set to typical geometry: at 10--20\,km the per-node disc-to-reach ratios on the calibration networks have medians of 1.3--1.5 and 99th percentiles of 1.7--3.4, so 2.5 exceeds the true ratio for all but a small tail (at most 2.5\% of live nodes in any calibration cell). The held-out network, checked after the fact, sits in a similar range (medians 1.6--1.8, 99th percentiles up to 3.1, up to 5.2\% of live nodes above the deflation; \texttt{output/euclidean\_reach\_ratios.csv}). The consequence is asymmetric: over-deflation only oversamples, the cheap direction of error (Section~\ref{sec:pilot}), while the tail nodes are under-sampled.

The count is correct on average but blind to circuity and barriers alike. A node counts disc neighbours the network cannot deliver within the distance limit. The excess travel comes either from a severing feature, such as a river or railway, or from the ordinary indirectness (circuity) of street routes. The fixed deflation is calibrated to typical geometry, not to the tail, so it absorbs ordinary circuity but leaves the high-circuity nodes under-corrected. Figure~\ref{fig:disc_vs_reach} shows the mechanism at one Cary node: its 10\,km disc holds \barrierDiscCount{} nodes while the network reaches \barrierReach{}, because most of the disc population sits near the rim, beyond 10\,km of network travel, so the true ratio (\barrierRatio) exceeds the deflation (2.5) and the node is under-sampled. This error is systematic and identifiable, but it concentrates on the 2.5--5.2\% of live nodes whose disc population lies far along the network, a group a map count cannot distinguish from typical nodes. That tail is too small to move a network-level rank correlation, but it distorts the estimates for the nodes it hits, so the rung is judged by the single-node mechanism of Figure~\ref{fig:disc_vs_reach} rather than by a network-level accuracy score.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig14_disc_vs_reach.pdf}
\caption{Ablation rung 2: Euclidean disc against network reach at 10\,km for the Cary node with the largest disc-to-reach ratio. The disc (dashed circle) contains \barrierDiscCount{} nodes; the network traversal from the node reaches \barrierReach{} (orange), and the solid line marks the smoothed boundary of the reached set. Grey nodes lie inside the disc but beyond 10\,km of network travel. No single barrier severs the eastern block: the exclusion is the accumulation of ordinary path circuity over a disc population concentrated near the rim, at straight-line distances of 7--10\,km from the node. The 2.5 deflation absorbs typical circuity; here the ratio rises to \barrierRatio{} and the node is under-sampled. The palest points are network nodes outside the disc, shown for context.}
\label{fig:disc_vs_reach}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Rung 3: measure reach on the network}

The pilot poll of Section~\ref{sec:pilot} travels on the network itself, so barriers, dead ends, and disconnected fringes are priced into the hit counts, and the confidence bounds convert the remaining uncertainty into oversampling rather than under-sampling. This rung is the method; there is nothing to ablate. Its results are the subject of Section~\ref{sec:validation}.

%==============================================================================
\section{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We validate on four real-world street networks spanning the urban density range, each built from official open road-network data. \emph{Greater London} (Ordnance Survey Open Roads; \glaNnodes{} live nodes) and \emph{Greater Madrid} (the official \emph{Red Viaria} road network; \madridNnodes{} live nodes) are dense metropolitan networks. \emph{Cary, NC} (US Census TIGER/Line; \caryNnodes{} live nodes; mean node degree $\approx 2.5$) is a low-density planned suburb in the Raleigh region. \emph{The Woodlands, TX} (US Census TIGER/Line; \woodlandsNnodes{} live nodes; mean node degree $\approx 2.5$) is a master-planned suburb north of Houston with a strongly dendritic (tree-like, cul-de-sac-heavy) street pattern. Each network is analysed within a \glaBuffer{}\,km buffer (Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}); in every case the live study area is delimited by the administrative boundary geocoded from OpenStreetMap via OSMnx \citep{Boeing2017}, independently of the road-geometry source.

The tolerance $\varepsilon$ was calibrated on Cary and the reach deflation of Section~\ref{sec:euclidean} on the calibration networks, so The Woodlands plays no part in selecting the accuracy parameters and serves as the out-of-sample accuracy test. The one constant set from timings on all four networks is the work-test margin $\gamma$, which affects which distances sample, and hence timing, but not the values of sampled estimates (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}). The margin is not load-bearing for the held-out sampled evidence: the held-out 20\,km betweenness cell runs at \woodlandsAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ with the pilot's cost included, a realised cost below a tenth of exact, so the sampling decision for that cell is insensitive to the margin's value.

Ground truth uses all sources ($p = 1$) and is deterministic. All timings are wall-clock on one workstation (Apple M5 Pro, 18 cores, 48\,GB memory); exact and sampled runs use the same parallel traversal code. Each speedup divides the exact reference time, recorded when the ground truth was built, by the mean sampled runtime. Exact and sampled runs were therefore timed in separate sessions on the same machine, so the smallest ratios (the 5\,km betweenness cells, at \madridAdaptiveFiveKmSpeedupB$\times$ to \glaAdaptiveFiveKmSpeedupB$\times$) carry the most session-to-session uncertainty; the mode decisions and the 10--20\,km gains do not depend on them.

The validation runs each metric at each distance as a separate single-metric call (\texttt{closeness\_shortest}, \texttt{betweenness\_shortest}), so the work test's mode is recorded per metric and every sampled cell pays a full pilot (Section~\ref{sec:worktest} gives the pricing for joint calls). A multi-distance call shares one pilot across its distances and costs less. We report the mean over three random seeds; the largest inter-seed standard deviation in $\rho$ across all networks, metrics, and distances is \adaptiveMaxSeedStd.

\subsection{Accuracy and cost}

All four networks meet the $\rho \geq \targetRho$ target for both metrics at every distance from 1--20\,km (Figure~\ref{fig:adaptive_accuracy}; Table~\ref{tab:adaptive_validation} consolidates $\rho$ and measured wall-clock speedups). The minimum sampled value is $\rho = \adaptiveMinRho$, on the held-out network's 20\,km betweenness; distances the work test routed to exact computation equal the ground truth by construction (open markers in Figure~\ref{fig:adaptive_accuracy}). The inter-seed spreads (at most \adaptiveMaxSeedStd) are small enough that every individual seed also clears the target, and the held-out network passes everywhere with no additional tuning. Panel~C extends that network beyond 20\,km on a rebuilt 50\,km buffer; Section~\ref{sec:limitations} reports the frontier test.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig13_adaptive_accuracy.pdf}
\caption{Spearman $\rho$ vs.\ analysis distance under the per-node method: closeness (A) and betweenness (B) on the calibration networks, and the held-out network (C) extended to 50\,km. Open markers denote distances the work test routed to exact computation, where $\rho = 1$ by construction; filled markers are sampled; the rule holds in every panel. In C, diamonds beyond the divider are the frontier rebuild: the held-out network rebuilt with a 50\,km buffer (nine counties), a larger graph, so its points are not joined to the 20\,km-buffered lines. Colours and marker shapes in C denote metrics rather than networks. On the frontier rebuild, sampled betweenness holds $\rho = 0.953$--$0.955$ at 30, 40, and 50\,km; closeness routes to exact throughout. The dashed line marks the $\rho = \targetRho$ target; every point on every network meets it.}
\label{fig:adaptive_accuracy}
\end{figure}

\input{tables/tab7_adaptive_validation}

The work test's decisions follow distance and density. No network samples at 1--2\,km, where traversals are cheap. On the metropolitan networks, betweenness sampling engages at 5\,km and closeness at 10\,km. On the suburbs, the closeness work test selects exact computation at every distance: their low live fractions ($\varphi = \caryLiveFraction$ and $\woodlandsLiveFraction$) make exact closeness cheap, and the method declines to sample it. Suburban betweenness, whose exact mode must run every node, samples at 10--20\,km.

Every sampled cell runs faster than exact computation, and the gain grows with distance (Table~\ref{tab:adaptive_validation}). The smallest speedup is \madridAdaptiveFiveKmSpeedupB$\times$ (Madrid, 5\,km betweenness), where the pilot and the per-source sampling arithmetic absorb most of the predicted saving; each sampled cell paid a full pilot (Section~\ref{sec:setup}). By 20\,km every network gains, with the sampled cells running \adaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupMin$\times$ to \adaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupMax$\times$.

On the cells both designs sample, the comparison with the canonical schedule turns on how a network's measured reach compares with the schedule's assumed reach. On London at 20\,km the method is faster: \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupC$\times$ and \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ against the schedule's \glaTwentyKmSpeedup$\times$ and \glaTwentyKmSpeedupBetweenness$\times$ (Tables~\ref{tab:validation}--\ref{tab:woodlands_validation}). London's measured reach exceeds the canonical assumption (Figure~\ref{fig:val_reach}), so the per-node probabilities sit below the schedule's fixed rate and the saving exceeds the pilot's cost. On Madrid at 20\,km the two designs run close together (\madridAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupC$\times$/\madridAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ against \madridTwentyKmSpeedup$\times$/\madridTwentyKmSpeedupBetweenness$\times$). On suburban betweenness the schedule is faster (\caryTwentyKmSpeedupBetweenness$\times$ and \woodlandsTwentyKmSpeedupBetweenness$\times$ against \caryAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ and \woodlandsAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$): its rate derives from an assumed reach above the suburbs' measured reach, so it draws fewer sources, and it pays no pilot and no separate pass per sampled distance. The same under-sampling fails the held-out closeness target (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}), and the schedule cannot detect the failure in advance.

Figure~\ref{fig:adaptive_comparison} places the method next to the canonical schedule of Section~\ref{sec:canonical}. Panels A and B show the 20\,km comparison per network for closeness and betweenness: the held-out closeness failure disappears, and the suburb closeness entries are computed exactly (open markers). Panel C decomposes betweenness $\rho$ by reach quartile on the held-out network: the upper three quartiles improve slightly under the per-node method, and the lowest-reach quartile shifts by a similar small amount in the opposite direction. Both designs show the same within-quartile depression: many low-reach streets have betweenness values at or near zero, their relative order is arbitrary, and no number of samples stabilises it.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig12_baseline_vs_adaptive.pdf}
\caption{Canonical schedule (ablation rung 1) versus the per-node method. A) Closeness and B) betweenness Spearman $\rho$ at 20\,km by network: the rung-1 held-out failure (Woodlands closeness, below the target line) is resolved; each network shows a paired grey and orange point on a truncated axis; per-node closeness entries are drawn as open markers where the work test selects exact computation. Per-node values are means over three seeds with inter-seed standard deviations of at most \adaptiveMaxSeedStd{} (Table~\ref{tab:adaptive_validation}). C) Betweenness $\rho$ within reach quartiles on the held-out network (Woodlands): the per-node method slightly improves the upper three quartiles, while the lowest-reach quartile shifts by a similar small amount in the opposite direction; within-quartile $\rho$ is depressed where tie-heavy near-zero betweenness values dominate a quartile, and the depression is shared by both designs, indicating a property of the value structure rather than a sample deficit. The $\rho = \targetRho$ line in panels A and B marks the network-wide target; panel C omits it because the target applies to the full ranking rather than to within-quartile correlations.}
\label{fig:adaptive_comparison}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Error structure}
\label{sec:error_structure}

Three views of the per-node errors show that the surviving error has little effect on rankings. Median relative error is roughly constant across reach deciles and lowest in the top decile (Figure~\ref{fig:error_vs_reach}): the highest-reach nodes carry the largest absolute residuals but the smallest relative ones. Their ranks barely move, because street-network centrality spans orders of magnitude and well-separated values tolerate small absolute errors. The spatial rank-shift maps (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_error}) show the shifts to be small, falling mostly on low-centrality nodes; the suburb closeness panels show zero shift because the work test computed them exactly. The decile-transition matrices (Figure~\ref{fig:decile_transition}) show most nodes remaining in their exact-computation decile, with the strongest stability in the upper deciles that identify the most central streets.

We apply the reach-quartile view of Figure~\ref{fig:adaptive_comparison}C to the sampled closeness cells on the metropolitan networks. Within-quartile rank correlations sit below the network-wide values: at 20\,km the four reach quartiles (lowest to highest) give $\rho$ = \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQOne, \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQTwo, \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQThree, and \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQFour{} on London, and \madridAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQOne, \madridAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQTwo, \madridAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQThree, and \madridAdaptiveTwentyKmRhoHQFour{} on Madrid; the minimum across all sampled closeness cells is \adaptiveClosenessQuartileMinRho{} (per-quartile detail is in the validation CSVs). Range restriction drives much of the depression: values within a quartile are close together, so a correlation computed inside the quartile magnifies reorderings that the network-wide ranking absorbs. The rank-shift statistic does not depend on value separation, and it stays small: the largest within-quartile median rank shift across the sampled closeness cells at 20\,km is \sampledClosenessQuartileShiftMax{} percentile points.

Paired statistics on the held-out network quantify the error geography against the canonical schedule at 20\,km. Under the schedule, closeness rank shifts cluster in space: the correlation between a node's rank shift and the mean shift of its eight nearest neighbours is \woodlandsBaselineNbrCorrC, and the mean rank displacement is \woodlandsBaselineRankDispC{} of the rank range. The method routes that cell to exact computation, so its residuals are zero. Figure~\ref{fig:rank_shift_paired} maps the pair. For betweenness the mean rank displacement is similar under the two designs (\woodlandsBaselineRankDispB{} vs \woodlandsAdaptiveRankDispB{}), while the neighbour correlation falls from \woodlandsBaselineNbrCorrB{} to \woodlandsAdaptiveNbrCorrB{}: errors remain, and they cluster less.

%==============================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
%==============================================================================

\subsection{Practical guidance}

In \cityseer{}, the user sets a single parameter, the tolerance $\varepsilon$; the library polls the network, assigns per-node probabilities, and selects exact computation where sampling cannot pay, with no further input. Algorithm~\ref{alg:adaptive} gives the full procedure for other implementations.

The realised speedup depends on distance, the live fraction, and network size. Distance matters most, because gains concentrate at long thresholds: at 20\,km London runs \glaAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupC--\glaAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ faster, Madrid \madridAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupC--\madridAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$, and suburban betweenness \caryAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ on Cary and \woodlandsAdaptiveTwentyKmSpeedupB$\times$ on the held-out network (Section~\ref{sec:validation}). The live fraction governs closeness: a study area with a small live fraction (a deep buffer around a compact boundary) sees little closeness benefit at any distance, because exact closeness already runs so few sources, so the work test routes suburban closeness to exact computation at a cost of the exact time plus the pilot poll. Network size sets a floor: below about 1{,}000 nodes exact computation completes in seconds and sampling is unnecessary.

Precision and speed trade off through the tolerance $\varepsilon$: halving it quadruples the required samples. Tightening to $\varepsilon = 0.04$ raises the sampled work by a factor of $(0.05/0.04)^2 \approx 1.6$ and lowers the realised speedup accordingly, whereas a looser $\varepsilon = 0.08$--$0.1$ buys speed for exploratory work at some cost to ranking accuracy. Betweenness bounds how loose $\varepsilon$ can go: closeness either samples with wide margins or routes to exact computation, whereas betweenness has heavier-tailed contributions and no per-source bound, so it is the first metric to degrade. On an unfamiliar network type, a check against exact computation at one long distance (10\,km, say) confirms $\rho > \targetRho$ before a full analysis commits to the sampled path.

\subsection{What the guarantee does and does not cover}
\label{sec:guarantee_scope}

The Hoeffding bound controls absolute error for the idealised survey of Section~\ref{sec:bound}; the validation measures whether the \emph{ranking} of nodes is preserved, and no formal bound connects the two.

Three factors make the bound loose in practice. First, Hoeffding's inequality uses only the range of contributions and ignores their much smaller variance. Second, the failure-budget allocation treats node-level errors as independent, though they are positively correlated. Third, rank preservation is more forgiving than additive error: centrality values span several orders of magnitude, so small absolute errors rarely reorder well-separated nodes, and the highest-centrality nodes are estimated most precisely (Section~\ref{sec:error_structure}). The bound is therefore conservative on all but the sparsest catchments, and the confidence-bound machinery of the pilot pushes the remaining uncertainty toward oversampling. The default $\varepsilon$ retains its additive-tolerance role in the bound, but its value was chosen by rank-fidelity calibration on Cary (Section~\ref{sec:canonical}), so the pair $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ describes a conservative operating point rather than a certified additive error.

\subsection{Scope and limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The method applies to shortest-path (metric) distance. Angular (simplest-path) distance \citep{Turner2007} does not satisfy the subpath optimality assumed in the betweenness derivation and remains to be tested. Validation spans dense European metropolitan networks and two low-density US suburbs; morphologies outside this range (informal settlements, gridiron megacities) are untested.

The main validation ends at 20\,km, the largest threshold the buffered network extents support. A frontier test rebuilds the held-out network with a 50\,km buffer and extends the distance axis: the work test routes closeness to exact computation at 30--50\,km, and sampled betweenness holds $\rho = 0.953$--$0.955$ through 30, 40, and 50\,km at speedups of 13--25$\times$ (\texttt{output/woodlands\_frontier.csv}). The decline in $\rho$ with distance flattens just above the target rather than crossing it.

Rank-based evaluation has no formal bridge from the additive bound, and betweenness has no per-source bound; both are validated rather than proven. The sampled closeness evidence comes from the metropolitan networks, because on the suburbs the work test routes closeness-only calls to exact computation at every distance; the held-out sampled evidence is therefore betweenness. A joint call can nevertheless sample suburban closeness (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}), and a supplementary check covers that configuration: forcing the sampled closeness path past the work test at 20\,km gives $\rho = \caryForcedClosenessRho$ on Cary and \woodlandsForcedClosenessRho{} on the held-out network against the exact ground truth, with every seed above the target (three seeds each; \texttt{output/forced\_closeness.csv}).

Two residual effects survive the design. The first is the pilot's tail risk: a node the poll happens to hit unusually often has its catchment overestimated and is under-sampled, with probability bounded by $\alpha$; the other error directions are safe, because a node the poll never hits is censused and the probability floor bounds the weights. The second is the betweenness quartile gradient of Section~\ref{sec:validation}, which improves under the method but does not vanish. A diagnostic on the held-out network at 20\,km traces this gradient to the high-traffic streets. For each node we count how many of the 400 pilot traversals pass through it; nodes crossed by 100 or more shift by a median of 1.7 and a 90th percentile of 9.6 percentile points, while the low-traffic periphery holds stable. The surviving noise is therefore the ordering of high-traffic streets, driven by contribution concentration, where a few origins dominate an arterial's value.

Natural extensions include a concentration-aware pilot for betweenness, validation on angular distance and a broader range of morphologies, online stopping criteria \citep{Borassi2019}, and variance-aware bounds \citep{Pellegrina2023}.

\subsection{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

Table~\ref{tab:bounds_comparison} summarises existing sampling approaches, grouped by computational primitive; \citet{Matta2019} provide a comprehensive empirical comparison for global betweenness.

Prior methods differ from ours on two axes: they set one network-wide precision target rather than a per-catchment one, and most estimate a single metric rather than sharing one source sample across both. \emph{Source-sampling} selects a subset of nodes and traverses the network from each. \citet{Brandes2007} established this approach empirically for both closeness and betweenness; \citet{Geisberger2008} refined betweenness estimation with distance-weighted corrections; \citet{Bader2007} used adaptive sampling with per-vertex guarantees. \emph{Path-sampling} \citep{Riondato2016, Riondato2018, Borassi2019, Pellegrina2023} draws random source--target pairs and computes one shortest path per sample; it applies only to betweenness, each sample updates only one path, and the set of admissible pairs depends on local morphology, so it does not adapt easily to localised analysis. Within this family, ABRA \citep{Riondato2018} adapts its sample size progressively through Rademacher averages, again to a global additive target. Bounded-distance estimands do appear within path-sampling: \citet{Riondato2016} extend their guarantee to a $k$-bounded-distance betweenness variant, though the precision target remains uniform over the network. The remaining methods in Table~\ref{tab:bounds_comparison} target global (unbounded) centrality and adapt their sample counts, where adaptive at all, to global estimation targets. Of these families, only source-sampling updates every reached node from a single traversal, so only it can serve both metrics from one sample sized to each catchment.

Sketch-based estimation is the closest prior for the closeness half of this requirement. All-distances sketches give every node a closeness estimate with a per-node relative-error guarantee \citep{Cohen2014, Cohen2015}, and because their estimators accept distance cutoffs they cover distance-bounded closeness. They still fall short on the rest: the sketches serve no betweenness and share no source sample across the two metrics, they estimate every node rather than selecting exact computation where a census is cheaper, and they require a dedicated sketch construction rather than the bounded Dijkstra traversals of standard centrality tooling.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Sampling approaches for centrality approximation. \emph{Source-sampling} traverses the network from each sampled node, updating all reached nodes. \emph{Path-sampling} draws individual shortest paths, updating only nodes along each path. Prior guarantees are uniform over the network; our approach uses distance-bounded reach $r$ instead of the full node count $n$ and serves both metrics from a single sample.}

%==============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
%==============================================================================

In localised network analysis, precision must follow the catchment. Each node's centrality is estimated over its own reach, so a sampling design that fixes one rate per network delivers unequal uncertainty across areas, which undermines cross-area comparison. The method presented here measures every catchment with a pilot poll, sizes each node's inclusion probability from a confidence bound on its reach, keeps estimates unbiased with inverse-probability weighting, and selects exact computation wherever a census is cheaper than a survey. One tolerance parameter governs precision. On four street networks spanning the urban density range, with one held out from accuracy calibration, the method preserves rank ($\rho \geq \adaptiveMinRhoFloor$) for closeness and betweenness at 1--20\,km; the work test selects exact computation for suburban closeness, so the sampled held-out evidence is betweenness. The ablation shows that assuming reach from distance fails on the held-out network exactly where its measured reach deficit predicts, and that map counts under-sample the nodes whose disc-to-reach ratio exceeds the fixed deflation. The remaining caveats are the rank-based evaluation, the absence of a per-source bound for betweenness, and the untested angular case.

The method is implemented in the open-source \cityseer{} Python package.\footnote{\href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}{github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api}} Analysis scripts and validation data are available in the repository's \texttt{analysis/sampling/} directory.

\section{Technical Details}

\paragraph{GLA network preprocessing.}

The Greater London Authority road network is sourced from Ordnance Survey Open Roads data (GeoPackage format).

Preprocessing steps:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Remove invalid and empty geometries
\item Explode multi-part geometries
\item Build NetworkX graph from edges
\item Remove filler nodes (degree-2 nodes that do not represent junctions)
\item Remove dangling nodes (dead-end segments $< 20\,$m)
\item Consolidate nearby nodes (threshold 1\,m)
\item Extract largest connected component
\end{enumerate}

Final network: \glaNtotal{} nodes, of which \glaNnodes{} are live within the boundary.

\paragraph{Madrid network.}

The Greater Madrid metropolitan network (\madridNnodes{} live nodes) is sourced from the official \emph{Red Viaria} road-network dataset for the Community of Madrid and preprocessed using the same consolidation pipeline as the GLA network. As for the other networks, the boundary delimiting the live area is geocoded from OpenStreetMap via OSMnx \citep{Boeing2017}.

\paragraph{Cary and Woodlands networks.}

The Cary, NC network (\caryNnodes{} live nodes) and The Woodlands, TX network (\woodlandsNnodes{} live nodes) are built from US Census TIGER/Line \emph{edges}, the topologically integrated road layer, which is natively noded at intersections (the cartographic \emph{roads} layer is not, and does not build a connected graph). Road edges (\texttt{ROADFLG = Y}) are loaded for every county intersecting the analysis area plus its \glaBuffer{}\,km buffer, then passed through the same consolidation pipeline as the GLA network. The live area is the municipal boundary; the surrounding region supplies the buffer.

\paragraph{Inverse-probability weighting.}
\label{sec:appendix_ht}

When nodes are sampled as sources with per-node inclusion probabilities $q_u$, each sampled contribution is scaled by the reciprocal of its own inclusion probability. This is a standard Horvitz--Thompson estimator \citep{Horvitz1952} and is unbiased whenever the probabilities are positive; unbiasedness does not depend on how the probabilities were chosen, so a rough pilot reach estimate affects only variance. The probability floor ($q_u \geq 0.01$) bounds the weights at 100, so a source $u$'s weighted term for target $v$ is at most $100/d(v,u) \leq 100/d_{\text{near}}$; this is the deployed-design analogue of the per-term bound $C_{\max}/k$ in the idealised argument of Section~\ref{sec:bound}. The source pool includes both live and buffer nodes (Section~\ref{sec:worktest}), ensuring that every node which contributes in exact mode has a positive probability of being sampled.

For closeness, sources enter the sample by independent per-node draws, and each source's contribution to a target is a fixed quantity (the inverse distance), so the per-source terms of the estimator are independent. For betweenness, the Brandes decomposition yields a fixed per-source term in the same way, so the same argument applies.

\paragraph{Betweenness over all routes.}
\label{sec:appendix_betw}

Betweenness counts shortest paths from every node, live or buffer: a path between two buffer nodes that passes through the interior legitimately credits the live intermediate it traverses, so excluding it would under-count boundary nodes. The \emph{live} designation therefore filters only which nodes' values are reported, not which sources run. Each ordered pair $(s,t)$ contributes with weight $\tfrac{1}{2}$ on undirected graphs (the two orderings of a symmetric pair are counted once between them) and $1$ on directed graphs; buffer-to-buffer routes through the interior are included. Under sampling this estimand is unchanged, and the Horvitz--Thompson $1/q_u$ scaling applies uniformly with no per-pair correction.

\paragraph{Implementation in \cityseer{}.}

The method is implemented in the \cityseer{} Python package (version 4.25+) and enabled via the \texttt{sample=True} flag. For each call, the library polls the network once (\texttt{estimate\_polled\_reach}), assigns per-node probabilities per distance (\texttt{compute\_node\_p}), and applies the work test of Section~\ref{sec:worktest} once per call and per distance. Distances routed to exact computation are batched into a single pass; each sampled distance runs its own pass under its own per-node probabilities. The \texttt{centrality\_shortest} function computes both closeness and betweenness from shared Dijkstra traversals in a single call:

\begin{verbatim}
from cityseer.metrics import networks

gdf = networks.centrality_shortest(
    network_structure,
    nodes_gdf,
    distances=[500,1000,2000,5000,10000,20000],
    sample=True
)
\end{verbatim}

Convenience wrappers (\texttt{closeness\_shortest}, \texttt{betweenness\_shortest}) compute a single metric each; the validation of Section~\ref{sec:validation} ran these wrappers, so they are the tested configuration. A joint \texttt{centrality\_shortest} call shares its traversals between the metrics and costs less; its mode decision can sample suburban closeness, the configuration checked by the forced-sampling run of Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

The defaults ($\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$, $\delta = \hoeffdingDelta$, poll level $\alpha = 0.1$, poll size $m = \min(n, \max(400, 0.025\,n))$, probability floor 0.01) are defined in \texttt{cityseer.sampling}, which also provides helper functions for custom workflows:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{estimate\_polled\_reach}: the pilot poll, returning lower-bound, point, and upper-bound reach estimates per distance
\item \texttt{compute\_node\_p}: per-node inclusion probabilities from reach estimates
\item \texttt{compute\_hoeffding\_p}: the reach-to-probability bound (Eq.~\ref{eq:hoeffding_k})
\item \texttt{compute\_distance\_p}: the canonical grid reference model of Section~\ref{sec:canonical}, retained for the ablation
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Reproducibility.}

All analysis scripts and validation results are available at \href{https://github.com/benchmark-urbanism/cityseer-api/tree/master/analysis/sampling}{analysis/sampling/}. The pipeline runs via \texttt{run\_all.py}: \texttt{01\_validate\_gla.py} through \texttt{04\_validate\_woodlands.py} build the exact ground truths and the canonical-schedule ablation record (the schedule is driven through the low-level API with an explicit per-distance probability, since the library's \texttt{sample=True} flag now runs the per-node method), \texttt{validate\_adaptive.py} runs the per-node method, and \texttt{05}--\texttt{10} generate the figures, macros, and tables. Supplementary checks run separately: \texttt{measure\_disc\_reach\_ratio.py} (Section~\ref{sec:euclidean}), \texttt{forced\_closeness\_check.py} (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}), and \texttt{epsilon\_sweep.py}. Each script's outputs are documented in its header.

\paragraph{Canonical schedule: per-distance ablation record.}

Tables~\ref{tab:validation}--\ref{tab:woodlands_validation} record the canonical schedule of Section~\ref{sec:canonical} on each network. Rows marked ``exact'' have $p \geq \varphi$, the schedule's fallback threshold; the rule is sized to exact closeness cost and applies to the whole call, so both metrics run exact in those rows and the schedule is not exercised. The held-out failure discussed in Section~\ref{sec:canonical} is the 20\,km closeness row of Table~\ref{tab:woodlands_validation}.

\paragraph{Spatial error distribution.}

The per-node rank-shift maps (Figure~\ref{fig:spatial_error}) and the decile-transition matrices (Figure~\ref{fig:decile_transition}) follow.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig7_rank_shift.png}
\caption{Spatial distribution of the per-node \emph{rank shift} under the per-node method at 20\,km ($\varepsilon = \hoeffdingEpsilon$): $|$pctile(true)$-$pctile(sampled)$|$ in percentile points, drawn as the hexbin median per cell on a fixed 0--10 white-to-red scale common to all panels; pale cells indicate small shifts, and cells with median shift above 10 saturate to the darkest colour. The largest cell medians are 14.5 percentile points (Madrid closeness) and 33.4 (Cary betweenness); saturated cells make up at most 0.2\% of each closeness panel and between 1.1\% and 8.4\% of each betweenness panel. Each panel shows a 20\,km by 20\,km window centred on the network, so the metropolitan networks extend beyond the frame. Rank shift is the quantity the design aims to preserve, and it stays small: shifts are larger for betweenness and fall mostly on low-centrality nodes, whose clustered values make ties easy to flip (Figure~\ref{fig:decile_transition}). The betweenness shifts are spatially diffuse; for London closeness (panel A) the larger shifts sit toward the edge of the mapped extent, away from the dense core, where closeness values lie closer together and ranks flip more easily. Panels C and D show zero shift because the work test routed the suburb closeness computations to exact mode; every cell of the network footprint sits at the zero end of the shared scale. An absolute-residual map would overstate the error, because residuals are largest where the values are largest, and those nodes scarcely change rank.}
\label{fig:spatial_error}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[p]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{figures/fig11_decile_transition.pdf}
\caption{Decile transition matrices showing the proportion of nodes that remain in the same centrality decile (diagonal) or move to another decile (off-diagonal) under the per-node method at 20\,km: closeness and betweenness on the metropolitan networks (A--D) and betweenness on the suburbs (E, F). Each row sums to 100\%: the percentage of nodes in a true decile assigned to each sampled decile. The suburb closeness matrices are omitted: the work test computed those cells exactly, so every node stays in its true decile. Diagonal dominance is strongest in the upper deciles (high-centrality nodes). In the betweenness panels the modal move for the tie-heavy lower-middle deciles is one decile downward (true deciles 3--4 on the suburbs, and marginally so for true decile 4 on London); these deciles hold near-zero values whose sampled estimates re-order easily, so diagonal dominance does not hold there. Rank swaps among low-centrality nodes have minimal practical impact, and top-decile retention stays high throughout.}
\label{fig:decile_transition}
\end{figure}
